sessions.setting: Gowanus Arts Building, 4th floor hallway between their adjacent studios, Tuesday morning

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: Morning, Jun. I think I left my palette knife on your side of the tool rack again. Did you see it?

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Yeah, it's right here. I hung it back on the shared rack this morning when I opened up 4B.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: Thanks. I was in such a rush leaving 4A last night that I didn't even clean up properly.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: No worries. Having adjacent studios is nice, but I swear our shared tool rack is becoming more yours than mine. There are like seven brushes on there that are definitely not for metalwork.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: Guilty. I'll move some back to my side. Hey, did you hear that the building manager is raising studio fees again next quarter?

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Yeah, I got the email. This building on 3rd Avenue is still the best deal in Gowanus though. I looked at spaces in Bushwick and they're worse for twice the price.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: True. Plus being right next to you means I always have someone to complain to when I'm stuck on a painting.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: And I have someone who doesn't mind when I'm grinding metal at eleven at night.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: I mean, I mind a little. But the earplugs help.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Fair enough. Want coffee? I just made a pour-over.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: Always. Let me grab my mug from the studio.

sessions.setting: Jun's studio 4B at the Gowanus Arts Building, afternoon work session

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: Jun, come look at these photos. I just finished the Red Hook mural and I want your opinion.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: The one on Van Brunt Street? The warehouse?

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: Yeah, the 40-foot Brooklyn waterfront piece. It took me three weeks on scaffolding in the cold, but it's done.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Wow, that scale is incredible. The water reflections look like they're actually moving. How'd you manage the color gradient at the top?

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: A lot of layering. A lot of going back down the ladder and squinting from across the street. Anyway, I can finally focus on studio work now. The Joan Mitchell Foundation grant came through in January, fifteen thousand dollars, so I have some breathing room.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: That's huge, congratulations. You can actually buy materials without panicking for a while.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: Exactly. Speaking of money, didn't you win something from the Brooklyn Arts Council recently?

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Yeah, the emerging artist prize last September. Five thousand. It covered about three months of material costs. I spend most of my budget at the Gowanus scrapyards buying reclaimed industrial metal. That stuff's not cheap even when it's salvaged.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: Metal sculptures from scrapyard finds. There's something poetic about that.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: I like giving old things a second life. There's this stack of railroad spikes I found last week that I'm dying to weld into something.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: You and your welding. It's all sparks and noise over there every day.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Art isn't always quiet. Sometimes it screams.

sessions.setting: Ines's studio 4D at the Gowanus Arts Building, morning — Jun delivering a birthday gift

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Happy birthday, Ines! Close your eyes and come to the kiln room.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Jun, what did you do? You know you didn't have to get me anything.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Just trust me. Okay, open.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Oh my god. Is that a welding table? You built me a welding table?

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Custom-made for your kiln room. The top is quarter-inch steel plate, heat-resistant up to two thousand degrees. I figured you needed a proper surface for working with your glazes and firing tools.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Jun, this is incredible. The craftsmanship is beautiful. Look at those joints.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: I spent about three weeks on it. Wanted to get the height right for you, and I added a lower shelf for your glaze buckets.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: You even thought about the glaze storage. This is the best birthday gift I've ever gotten. Seriously.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Well, you spend half your life in Studio 4D mixing glazes, so you deserve a proper workspace.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: I was literally just working on a new batch of my Paprika glaze this morning. That copper-red reduction formula took me two years to perfect. Now I have a real surface to work on instead of that wobbly folding table.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: The wobbly table was a safety hazard. I was worried about you.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Thank you, Jun. Really. I'm going to make you the most beautiful ceramic piece you've ever seen as a thank-you.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: I'll hold you to that. Happy birthday.

sessions.setting: Shared darkroom on the 3rd floor of the Gowanus Arts Building, afternoon

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: Ines, are you done with the enlarger? I need to print a batch from the Ghana trip.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Almost. Give me five more minutes. I'm printing some documentation shots of a piece I fired at the Watershed Center back in September.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: The one in Maine? The big ceramic column?

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Yeah, the 4-foot column from the wood-fired anagama kiln. The surface came out with these incredible ash deposits that I want to document properly before I submit the photos for a grant application.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: That piece was stunning. I love that we share this darkroom and print station. It's the only reason I still shoot film.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Same. Having dedicated space on the 3rd floor is a luxury. Most photographers I know in Brooklyn don't have darkroom access at all.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: It's why I've been able to keep shooting my Accra work on film. I was in Ghana for three weeks in January photographing my extended family for the Diaspora Kitchen series.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: How was that? Going back to where your family's from?

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: Intense. Emotional. My grandmother's kitchen is nothing like what I grew up with in the Bronx, but the smells are exactly the same. That's what I'm trying to capture, that sensory continuity across generations and geography.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: That's beautiful, Zara. Okay, the enlarger's all yours. I'll clean up my side of the station.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: Thanks. I'll probably be here a couple more hours. These negatives need careful handling.

sessions.setting: BRIC Arts Media gallery in Fort Greene, evening setup for their upcoming exhibition

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: Okay, I think if we hang the large oils on the west wall and your photo series on the east, visitors will naturally move through the space in a narrative arc.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: I agree. The Thresholds concept is all about transitions, so the physical flow through the gallery should mirror that.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: Exactly. I can't believe BRIC actually gave us the space. Co-curating a show here in Fort Greene feels like a huge milestone.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: It is. We've been talking about doing something together since we figured out the Professor Venn connection.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: That still blows my mind. You took that summer intensive with Claudia at RISD in 2017, and she was my MFA thesis advisor. I had no idea until we both started at Gowanus.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: I remember her mentioning a promising painting student from Minneapolis during that summer workshop, but I never connected it to you until you showed me your thesis catalog.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: Small world. Claudia always pushed us to think about thresholds, liminal spaces, in-between states. So this show title felt right.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: It's a direct homage to her teaching. She'd be proud, I think.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: She would. I emailed her an invitation. She said she'll try to make the opening in April.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: That would be amazing. Okay, let's figure out the lighting. Your oils need warm spots, and my prints need even, diffused light.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: Let's walk through it one more time. We've got less than two weeks before opening night.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: Two weeks. We can do this.

sessions.setting: Maren's studio 4A, lunchtime — Ines picking up painting supplies

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Hey Maren, is it okay if I grab some of that Williamsburg cadmium orange? I need it for an oil-based glaze batch.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: Of course. You know where the supply shelf is. I buy the Williamsburg paints in bulk from New York Central Art Supply, so there's always extra.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: You're a lifesaver. Buying single tubes of oil paint at retail prices would bankrupt me. The bulk rate makes such a difference.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: That's why I started buying in bulk in the first place. It's my primary medium, oil paint, so it made sense. And now you benefit too.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: I've been experimenting with oil-based glazes on my ceramics. It gives the surface this depth that standard ceramic glazes can't achieve. My training at Alfred didn't really cover this kind of crossover.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: Alfred University? That's your MFA, right?

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Yeah, MFA from Alfred in 2022. Before that I did my BFA in ceramics at the Cleveland Institute of Art. Neither program really explored oil-ceramic hybrids. I'm kind of inventing as I go.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: That's the best kind of art, honestly. No textbook, just experimentation.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Spoken like a true painter. Okay, I'm taking the cadmium orange and a bit of the burnt sienna if that's alright.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: Take whatever you need. Just let me know when stocks get low so I can reorder.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Will do. Thanks, Maren. I owe you a set of mugs.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: I will absolutely take you up on that.

sessions.setting: Greenpoint Gallery, late afternoon — visiting the space where their show was held

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: I still can't believe how well Fire and Form went. The gallery owner just told me they had more visitors in February than any other month this year.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Seriously? That two-person show at the Greenpoint Gallery might be the best thing either of us has done.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: The pairing made sense. Your welded steel structures next to my fired ceramic columns. Fire was the common element.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: That's what made the concept work. Both of us transform raw material through heat. Just different kinds of heat.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: You know, when I won the American Craft Council award back in November, the three thousand dollars, they specifically asked about my process. I told them about collaborating with a sculptor and how it pushed my thinking.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: That's great. The craft innovation award, right? For the Paprika glaze?

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Yeah. They loved the formula. But the conversation about cross-medium collaboration is what stuck with them. Where'd you study again? Sometimes I forget if you did the sculpture track or something broader.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: BFA in sculpture from the Pacific Northwest College of Art. Graduated in 2019 and moved straight to New York. Portland was great for learning, but the scene here is just on another level.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Cleveland was the same for me. Great education, but you have to be in New York to really push yourself.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Exactly. Hey, should we pitch the gallery on a follow-up show? Maybe expand the concept, bring in Maren and Zara too?

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: I love that idea. Let me talk to the owner next week.

sessions.setting: Sahadi's restaurant on Atlantic Avenue, Thursday morning brunch after the Thresholds opening week

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: I can't think of a better way to celebrate the show than brunch at Sahadi's. Their hummus plate is the reason I live in Brooklyn.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: You and this place. Every time I ask where you want to eat, it's Sahadi's.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: Because it's the best. The Atlantic Avenue location is perfect. Don't fight me on this.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: I'm not fighting. I'm just saying there are other restaurants. But the hummus is undeniably good. Okay, so Thresholds is officially open. How does it feel?

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: Surreal, honestly. When I was doing my MFA at RISD, graduating in 2018, I never imagined I'd be co-curating a show at BRIC six years later.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: I felt the same way finishing my MFA at ICP in 2020. Photography school doesn't exactly prepare you for gallery politics and exhibition logistics.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: ICP is such a great program though. Your documentary work has that editorial rigor that I think comes from that training.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: Thanks. And your painting has this physicality that you can only get from the RISD tradition. The two bodies of work complement each other perfectly in the show.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: The reviews have been kind. Did you see the Brooklyn Rail piece?

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: I did. They loved the juxtaposition. Oh, speaking of gear, I need to get my Mamiya serviced. The light meter on my Mamiya 7 II has been acting up, and I have a shoot next week.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: You still shooting everything on that medium format film camera? In 2024?

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: Film gives a quality that digital can't replicate. The grain, the tonal range. It's worth the extra work.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: I respect the commitment. More hummus?

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: Always more hummus.

sessions.setting: Socrates Sculpture Park in Long Island City, afternoon — Zara photographing Jun's installation

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: Jun, hold still. The light is hitting your piece perfectly right now.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Take as many as you need. I still can't believe the Socrates Sculpture Park fellowship came through. Having a 12-foot welded steel piece installed here is a dream.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: When does it officially open to the public?

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Later this month. The emerging artist fellows each get a site for the summer season. Mine's positioned to catch the afternoon sun, so the shadows shift throughout the day.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: That's very Richard Serra of you.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: I'll take that as the highest compliment. Serra is my favorite sculptor. His Torqued Ellipses at Dia Beacon literally changed how I think about space.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: I can see that influence in your work. The way you use negative space and scale. These photos are going to look great.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Thanks for doing this, by the way. I need good documentation for grant applications. What about your own projects? How's the Diaspora Kitchen series going?

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: It's expanding. I'm now documenting the cooking traditions of 40 immigrant families across all five boroughs. The scope keeps growing because every family leads me to another one.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Forty families? That's an enormous project.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: It is. But my hero, Gordon Parks, always said you should photograph the story that only you can tell. This is mine.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Gordon Parks is a solid north star. His work at Life magazine was incredible.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: He proved that documentary photography can be both art and activism. That's what I'm going for. Okay, move two steps to the left. I want the Manhattan skyline in the background.

sessions.setting: Maren's apartment on Dean Street in Boerum Hill, evening dinner with Jun

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Nice place. The third-floor walkup keeps you in shape, I bet.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: Yeah, hauling canvases up three flights on Dean Street is basically my workout. Kai keeps saying we should move somewhere with an elevator, but I love Boerum Hill too much.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Kai has a point though. My loft in Bushwick on Knickerbocker Avenue is ground floor, which is great because I use it as overflow workspace for smaller pieces.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: That's handy. A live-work space. How do you keep metal dust off your furniture?

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: I don't, honestly. It's everywhere. The couch has a permanent iron patina at this point.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: Charming. How'd you get here tonight? The bike rack downstairs is empty.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Subway. I only drive the van when I'm hauling sculpture. Speaking of bikes, yours was locked up outside the building, right? The turquoise one?

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: My Bianchi road bike, yeah. I ride it to the studio every day. It's faster than the train from Boerum Hill to Gowanus.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: A turquoise Bianchi. Very on-brand for you. Elegant, a little European. Like your paintings.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: I'll take that as a compliment. So, dinner? I'm making pasta.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Sounds great. But I can't stay too late. I've got kendo at the Brooklyn Kendo Club on Flatbush tomorrow morning. Well, technically I go every Wednesday and Saturday evening, but this week they moved Saturday's session to Wednesday morning.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: Kendo? You do kendo?

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Since high school. It keeps me disciplined. Plus, swinging a shinai is oddly similar to swinging a hammer. Same focus, same precision.

sessions.setting: G train, riding together from Crown Heights toward Gowanus, late morning

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: I always forget you live so close to the studio. Five-minute walk, right?

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Yeah, my converted warehouse apartment in Gowanus is just down the block. I could practically throw a clay ball from my window and hit the building.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: I'm jealous. I take the G train from Crown Heights every day. It's about a 20-minute commute from Nostrand Avenue.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Crown Heights is nice though. Good food, good energy.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: It is. And my rent-stabilized apartment means I can actually afford to be an artist in this city. If I ever lose that lease, I'm done.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Same fear, different situation. I rely on the Brooklyn Flea Market for income. I sell pottery there on weekends in Dumbo. Mugs, bowls, plates. Functional stuff.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: How does that go?

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Surprisingly well. I average about eight hundred dollars on a good Saturday. It's not glamorous, but it keeps the studio rent paid.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: Eight hundred on a Saturday? That's solid. I should come by sometime.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Please do. I'll give you the friends-and-family discount. Which is just regular price but with a smile.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: Ha. This is our stop. Ready for another day in the darkroom?

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Always. I've got prints to make.

sessions.setting: Gowanus Arts Building, Jun's welding workshop on the first Saturday of the month

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: How many students do you have today?

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Eight. It's the introductory welding workshop I run on the first Saturday of each month here at the building. This group is all beginners, so it'll be basic torch work and safety.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: I love that you do this. I teach my weekend oil painting workshop at the Brooklyn Art Center on Atlantic Avenue, so I know how rewarding it is.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Teaching forces you to articulate things you do on instinct. It makes my own work better.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: Exactly. Last week one of my students asked me why I chose oil over acrylic, and I found myself giving this twenty-minute answer about viscosity, layering, and light refraction that I'd never consciously articulated before.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Where are you from originally? I always forget. Somewhere in the Midwest, right?

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: Portland, Oregon. Wait, no, that's you. I'm from Minneapolis. But I speak Norwegian too, from my parents, so people sometimes assume I'm Scandinavian-born.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Right, right. Minneapolis. I'm Portland, Oregon. Moved to New York in 2019 after finishing art school. Five years here and I still sometimes miss the Pacific Northwest.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: I miss Minneapolis winters, weirdly. There's a quality of light in January that I can't replicate here.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Okay, that's just masochism. Portland rain I miss. Minneapolis blizzards? No thanks.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: To each their own. Go teach your students. I'll be in my studio if you need anything.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Will do. And if you hear screaming, it's just someone touching a hot weld for the first time.

sessions.setting: Prospect Park, Saturday afternoon, walking after Zara's community photo walk

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: That was incredible. Thirty-five people showed up for the photo walk today. I honestly expected maybe fifteen.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: Thirty-five! The community photo walk through Prospect Park actually doubled your projection?

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: Yeah. People are hungry for this kind of thing. I had participants from teenagers to retirees, all just walking and shooting together. It was beautiful.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: You organized the whole thing yourself?

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: With help from some of my students at the Bronx Documentary Center. A few of them came down to assist. Speaking of background, I've been thinking about family a lot lately.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: How so?

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: The Diaspora Kitchen project keeps bringing me back to my roots. My parents came from Accra in 1990. I grew up in Morrisania in the Bronx, speaking English and Twi at home, French at school. Three languages before age ten.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: Three languages is impressive. I only have two. English and Norwegian. My parents emigrated from Bergen, Norway in 1988 and settled in Minneapolis.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: Bergen? That's beautiful country. Have you been?

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: Many times. My whole extended family is still there. My dad, Erik, is a carpenter in Minneapolis though. He builds custom furniture. I think I got my sense of scale from watching him work with wood my whole childhood.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: That makes sense. From carpentry to murals, it's all about physical making at a human scale.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: Exactly. Dad would love it if I came back to Minneapolis, but New York is where the work is.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: Amen to that. Want to grab something to eat? I'm starving from all that walking.

sessions.setting: Ines's studio 4D, afternoon — working on pieces while chatting

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: My mom called again this morning. She's convinced I'm not eating enough.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Moms. What does your mom do again?

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Katalin teaches Hungarian language and literature at Case Western Reserve in Cleveland. So she's an academic who can't understand why her daughter chose to make pots for a living instead of getting a PhD.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: I get that. My dad's an architect at ZGF Architects in Portland. Hiroshi Takeda, very serious, very structured. When I told him I was going into sculpture instead of architecture, he didn't speak to me for a week.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: A week? That's rough.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: He came around eventually. He actually helped me design the structural supports for some of my larger pieces. Architecture training has its uses.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: That's sweet. My parents came from Budapest in '93, so they have that immigrant drive of wanting their kids to have stable careers. Art is... not that.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Growing up in Tremont or somewhere else in Cleveland?

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Tremont, yeah. It's this artsy neighborhood on the west side. Actually a great place to grow up if you're going to end up as a ceramicist. There were studios everywhere.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: That explains a lot. Do you speak Hungarian at home still?

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Fluently. English and Hungarian. My mom insisted. She said losing your language is losing your identity. I'm grateful now, even if I resented the Saturday Hungarian school as a kid.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Same with my Japanese. English and Japanese, both fluent. My grandparents in Tokyo would've disowned me otherwise.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: The bilingual artist club. We should get jackets made.

sessions.setting: Zara's studio 4C at the Gowanus Arts Building, afternoon — Zara showing Maren her New Yorker prints

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: Come in, come in. I just got the printed copies delivered to Studio 4C this morning.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: The New Yorker issue? Let me see!

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: The photo essay on Ghanaian immigrant families in Flatbush. Published in the June photo issue. Eight pages. I still can't believe it.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: Zara, these are breathtaking. The intimacy in these kitchen scenes is unreal.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: Thank you. Each family let me into their home for multiple days. That trust is everything.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: I know the feeling of a project finally landing. I just sold Fjord Memory last week. A private collector paid eighty-five hundred for it.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: The large-scale oil painting? The one with the Norwegian coastline that was in the Thresholds show?

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: That's the one. It's bittersweet. I spent months on it, and now it's going to someone's living room. But eighty-five hundred dollars means I can keep making work.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: That's the deal we make. Speaking of Norway, when did you last go back?

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: Oslo, July 2023. Two weeks studying Edvard Munch's techniques at the Munch Museum. His layering method influenced the Fjord Memory piece directly.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: I can see that. The emotional density in the brushwork. Munch is all over it, but in a good way.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: That trip changed how I approach oil. Standing in front of The Scream in person is different from any reproduction.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: Every artist needs those pilgrimages. Mine was Ghana. Yours was Oslo.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: Now I need to channel all of it into the new work. October is coming fast.

sessions.setting: Zara's apartment in Crown Heights, brunch visit on a Thursday morning

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: Thanks for coming all the way out to Crown Heights. I know it's a trek from Gowanus.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: It's fine. I speak English and Hungarian, not twenty languages, but I can navigate the subway. How's your mom doing?

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: Abena's good. Busy as always. She's a registered nurse at Montefiore Medical Center in the Bronx, so her shifts are unpredictable. I worry about her working so hard.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Healthcare workers are a different breed. My mom just grades papers and complains about her students. Yours is saving lives.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: She'd love hearing that. What are you working on these days? Besides the regular pottery for the Flea?

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: I've been thinking a lot about what I learned in Shigaraki. I traveled to the Shigaraki Ceramic Cultural Park in Japan in August 2023 to study traditional wood-fired kiln techniques. The Japanese approach to wood firing is completely different from what we do in the West.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: How so?

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: They fire for days, sometimes weeks. The ash from the wood creates these natural glazes on the surface that you can't replicate any other way. It's about surrendering control to the fire. That experience is driving everything I'm doing now.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: I love that. Surrendering control. I feel the same way about documentary work. You can't stage truth. Speaking of truth, I need to prepare for my class tonight.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Class?

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: I teach a documentary photography course at the Bronx Documentary Center on 151st Street every Thursday evening. It keeps me connected to the community I grew up in.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: That's really meaningful, Zara. Going back to the Bronx to teach.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: The kids there remind me of myself at that age. Lots of stories to tell, not enough people showing them how.

sessions.setting: Flatiron District, lobby of Meridian Labs office building, afternoon — Jun overseeing installation of his commissioned sculpture

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Careful with the base! Tilt it ten degrees to the left. That's it.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: This piece is stunning, Jun. Twelve thousand dollars well earned.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Thanks for helping with the install. Meridian Labs wanted something that evoked innovation and movement. I think the spiraling steel captures that.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: It does. A commissioned sculpture for a tech company lobby in the Flatiron District. That's a big deal.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: The money helps. I can finally replace some worn-out equipment. Plus it validates that corporate commissions can be artistically genuine, not just decoration.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: Absolutely. How did you even get the piece here?

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: My white Ford Transit cargo van. The 2017 model. It's basically a mobile studio at this point. I use it to transport sculptures to every exhibition, every install.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: I need something like that for when I do murals. Can't exactly strap a scaffold to a Bianchi.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: You can borrow the van anytime. What are you working on next?

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: The Minus Space solo show. Twelve new paintings for their gallery in Dumbo, opening in October. It's the biggest solo opportunity I've had.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Minus Space? That's a serious gallery. Congratulations.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: Thanks. I'm excited and terrified. Twelve paintings by October. I need to basically live in the studio for the next two months.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: You should take a break at some point though. Have you been to Dia Beacon recently? Sometimes stepping away helps.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: Dia Beacon is my favorite museum. The large-scale installations there always reset my brain. Maybe I'll take a day trip before the crunch gets too intense.

sessions.setting: Frankel's Delicatessen on Greenpoint Avenue, Tuesday lunch

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: I've been craving Frankel's all week. Their pastrami sandwich is the one thing that gets me through a long firing cycle.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: You and your pastrami. I'm more of a Peppa's Jerk Chicken on Flatbush person, but I have to admit this is good.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Peppa's is great too. But Frankel's on Greenpoint Avenue is sacred ground to me. It reminds me of the delis in Cleveland growing up.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: Fair enough. So what have you been up to besides firing ceramics?

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Teaching, actually. I have a hand-building ceramics class on Tuesday evenings at the 92nd Street Y in Manhattan. The commute is annoying, but the students are wonderful.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: The 92nd Street Y? That's a prestigious teaching gig.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: It is. Mostly adults who want to learn something new. Very different from gallery work. What about you? Any big news?

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: Well, I've been meaning to tell you. Remember the W. Eugene Smith Memorial Fund Grant I won last October? The forty thousand?

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: How could I forget? Forty thousand dollars for Diaspora Kitchen. That was huge.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: So the fund is now asking me to do a presentation on the project at their annual symposium. They want me to speak about the methodology behind the series.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Zara, that's incredible. You deserve every bit of recognition you're getting.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: Thanks. It still feels unreal sometimes. A kid from Morrisania presenting at a W. Eugene Smith event.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: A kid from Tremont selling pottery at the Brooklyn Flea. We're all just making it up as we go.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: Cheers to that. Pass the mustard.

sessions.setting: Gowanus Arts Building rooftop, late afternoon — inspecting the kiln construction site

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Okay, so the foundation is laid. The firebrick inner chamber will go here, and the chimney stack will be on the east side for draft.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: You're really building a wood-fired kiln on the rooftop of this building? Have you cleared this with the landlord?

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Cleared, permitted, and fire-department approved. This custom outdoor wood-fired kiln has been my dream for two years. It should be completed by December.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: That's ambitious. How big?

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Big enough to fire architectural-scale pieces. The design is based on what I studied in Shigaraki. Oh, and I got some amazing news. I was selected for the Ceramic Arts Residency at the Archie Bray Foundation in Helena, Montana for summer 2025.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Archie Bray? That's one of the most prestigious ceramic residencies in the country. Congratulations!

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Thank you. I'm thrilled. Montana in summer will be a nice change from Brooklyn. What about you? Any travel plans?

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Not until winter. I went to Naoshima Island in Japan last December. Visited the Chichu Art Museum and Benesse House. It was transformative.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Naoshima! I've always wanted to go there. The Tadao Ando architecture alone is worth the trip.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: The Monet room in the Chichu museum is indescribable. Natural light only. The paintings seem to float. It made me rethink how I think about displaying sculpture.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Japan keeps calling both of us back, doesn't it?

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: It does. Hey, want to grab dinner after this? I've been craving Okonomi on Metropolitan Avenue. Their traditional Japanese breakfast-for-dinner is exactly what I need.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Breakfast for dinner? I'm in. Let me wash the clay off my hands first.

sessions.setting: Gowanus Arts Building, 4th floor common area — group gathering to celebrate recent achievements and plan next steps

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: Alright, everyone. We're all here. First round of drinks is on me since my solo show at Minus Space opens in two weeks and I'm too nervous to do anything else.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: You'll be great. And I need to tell you all something. I've been building a series of kinetic wind sculptures made from salvaged copper pipe for a group show at Pioneer Works in Red Hook.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: Pioneer Works? Jun, that's a fantastic venue. When does it open?

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: November. The copper pipe comes from demolition sites around Gowanus. Same sourcing philosophy as my steel work, just a different material. My dad the architect would appreciate the material reuse angle. The idea actually came from watching the wind move through the trees at Socrates Sculpture Park. I realized I wanted my work to respond to its environment, not just occupy space.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: I love that. Speaking of new directions, I have news too. I've been invited to exhibit twenty prints from Diaspora Kitchen at the Aperture Foundation gallery in Chelsea. Opening in November.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: Aperture Foundation? Zara, that's one of the most important photography galleries in the world. You must be thrilled.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: Thrilled and terrified. I've been trying not to think about it too hard or I'll panic.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Don't panic. Your work is extraordinary. And I have something to share too. I've been studying Peter Voulkos's approach to breaking ceramic conventions. He's my favorite ceramic artist, and his influence is all over the new architectural pieces I'm developing.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: Voulkos was a genius. The way he treated clay like an Abstract Expressionist treated paint.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Exactly. I want that freedom in my large-scale work. The pieces I'll fire in the new rooftop kiln are going to be completely different from anything I've done before.

turns.speaker: maren
turns.text: Look at us. A painter, a sculptor, a photographer, and a ceramicist, all on the same floor of the same building, all pushing in new directions. The Gowanus Arts Building, fourth floor.

turns.speaker: zara
turns.text: It's special what we have here. Studios 4A through 4D. We should do a group show someday. All four of us.

turns.speaker: jun
turns.text: I'm in. One hundred percent.

turns.speaker: ines
turns.text: Same. Let's make it happen.
